title: Hymn 5, sound: karau benantee
hookLine: karau benantee sunahu mere meetaa (Gauri Purbi M5, ang 13)

lines: LISTEN, CAN I ASK YOU SOMETHING?
THE LAST HYMN LOWERS ITS VOICE.
cards: There's a tone people use when something really matters. Not a speech, not a lecture. A friend leaning across the table, lowering their voice: listen, can I ask you something?
It's the tone that gets a phone put down. The last hymn of Sohila opens in that voice. After the crowded city of the fourth hymn, the fifth doesn't raise its voice at all.
It turns to the listener, calls them friend, and asks for attention. And it's a third Guru's voice: Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru.

teach.h: KARAU BENANTEE: I MAKE A REQUEST.
teach.b: Here's the first line: karau benantee, sunahu mere meetaa. Word by word. Karau: I make, I offer.
Benantee: a humble request, a plea; the everyday Punjabi word benti means the same, a heartfelt request.
Sunahu: listen. Mere: my. Meetaa: friends.
So: I make a request; listen, my friends. Notice who's speaking to whom. Guru Arjan compiled the Adi Granth, the scripture Sikhs now honor as the Guru Granth Sahib.
He could have opened with authority.

Instead he opens like someone asking a favor, and calls the listeners friends, not followers. Then the line goes on, and the request turns out to be urgent. In paraphrase: this is the time to serve the holy.
We'll open that tomorrow. For now, see the shape Sohila has built.
Five hymns, three Gurus. Guru Nanak wrote the first three: the house of praise, the six schools and one sun, the sky's aarti.

Guru Ram Das wrote the fourth, the city full of thieves. Guru Arjan wrote this fifth. The first is in a form of Raag Gauri, the second in Asa, the third in Dhanasri, and the last two share Gauri Purbi.
A little anthology in one night prayer, ending not with a doctrine but with a friend saying: please, listen.

how: This is the fifth and final hymn of Kirtan Sohila, which Sikhs recite each night before sleep; in gurdwaras, the Guru Granth Sahib is then laid to rest for the night.

o: a humble request, made the way a friend asks
a command given with a teacher's authority
a song of thanks after a prayer is answered

games.q: Sohila's five hymns — tap the pairs.

s: Sohila's five hymns are all by Guru Nanak
three are Guru Nanak's, one is Guru Ram Das's, and the last is Guru Arjan's.
the everyday Punjabi word benti means the same.
the last hymn addresses its listeners as followers

games.q: you compiled the scripture, and you're writing the last hymn of the night prayer. how does Guru Arjan open it?
o: with a humble request: listen, my friends.
games.why: karau benantee, sunahu mere meetaa: he asks, as a friend, for the listener's attention.

practice: Say the line once in an ordinary voice: karau benantee, sunahu mere meetaa. Then say it the way you'd speak to a close friend you were worried about, lower, slower, closer, and notice how different it sounds.
Sit and imagine it said to you, by someone who wants good for you, and if you pray, say Waheguru once, softly.

wordCard.voice: Benti, a humble request: Sohila's last hymn, by Guru Arjan in Raag Gauri Purbi, which opens with a plea, I make a request; listen, my friends.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: benti, a humble request; sung as benantee in the hymn's first line.

carryVoice: Your line: karau benantee. I make a request: a friend asking, not a boss ordering. Day four hundred thirty-two, done.

sources.ref: Gauri Purbi M5, Ang 13 (Kirtan Sohila, hymn 5)
